subject: Neurology
subtopic: Cranial nerve III, IV, VI palsies
vignette: A 65-year-old man with long-standing diabetes mellitus develops right ptosis and a right eye that rests 'down and out.' His pupil remains reactive to light and is equal in size to the left. The clinician diagnoses an ischemic oculomotor palsy.
question: Which of the following best explains why the pupil is spared in this patient?

options.text: Compression affects peripheral parasympathetic fibers first
Ischemia predominantly damages peripheral fibers on the nerve surface
The parasympathetic fibers run in the optic nerve, not CN III
Ischemia affects central motor fibers more than peripheral parasympathetic fibers
The sphincter pupillae is supplied by the sympathetic chain

explanation_correct: In diabetic CN III palsy, microvascular ischemia from sorbitol accumulation compromises the vasa nervorum on the outside of the nerve, reducing diffusion of oxygen and nutrients to the central (middle) motor fibers. The peripheral parasympathetic fibers are relatively spared, so the light reflex remains intact and the pupil is 'spared.' This contrasts with compressive lesions, which affect the superficial parasympathetic fibers first.

explanation_incorrect.A: Compression of peripheral parasympathetic fibers causes a blown pupil, as with a PCom aneurysm, not a pupil-sparing palsy.
explanation_incorrect.B: Ischemia affects the central fibers worst because the peripheral vasculature is compromised; the surface parasympathetic fibers are relatively preserved.
explanation_incorrect.C: Parasympathetic pupillary fibers travel with CN III to the ciliary ganglion, not in the optic nerve.
explanation_incorrect.E: The sphincter pupillae is parasympathetic; the sympathetic chain supplies the dilator pupillae.

educationalObjective: Ischemic CN III palsy is pupil-sparing because central motor fibers are more vulnerable than the peripheral parasympathetic fibers.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Cranial nerve III, IV, VI palsies
vignette: A 50-year-old woman develops sudden-onset severe headache and notices that her right pupil is dilated and unreactive to light. The right eye is displaced down and out with ptosis. Angiography reveals an aneurysm at the junction of the posterior communicating and internal carotid arteries.
question: Which of the following mechanisms best accounts for the dilated pupil in this patient?

options.text: Compression of peripheral parasympathetic fibers by the aneurysm
Microvascular ischemia of the central motor fibers
Interruption of sympathetic fibers along the internal carotid
Direct injury to the pretectal nuclei in the midbrain
Entrapment of the inferior rectus in an orbital floor fracture

explanation_correct: The parasympathetic fibers of CN III run on the periphery of the nerve, so they are the first affected by external compression such as a PCom aneurysm or uncal herniation. Loss of constrictor input to the sphincter pupillae produces a dilated, unreactive 'blown pupil,' often with down-and-out gaze. The sudden headache reflects the aneurysmal expansion or rupture.

explanation_incorrect.B: Ischemic injury to central motor fibers produces a pupil-sparing palsy, not a dilated unreactive pupil.
explanation_incorrect.C: Sympathetic interruption would cause miosis and ptosis (Horner syndrome), the opposite of a blown pupil.
explanation_incorrect.D: A pretectal lesion would disrupt the afferent light reflex but would not produce a unilateral dilated pupil with down-and-out gaze from CN III compression.
explanation_incorrect.E: Inferior rectus entrapment from a blowout fracture limits upward gaze and causes cheek numbness, not a dilated pupil.

educationalObjective: Compressive CN III lesions affect superficial parasympathetic fibers first, producing a blown pupil and down-and-out gaze.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Cranial nerve III, IV, VI palsies
vignette: A 35-year-old man has trouble going down stairs and reading because he cannot look downward. The right eye sits higher than the left, and he compensates by tilting his head to the left. There is no ptosis and the pupils are equal.
question: Which nerve is most likely injured?

options.text: Right CN III
Right CN VI
Right CN IV
Left CN IV
Left CN III

explanation_correct: CN IV innervates the superior oblique, which intorts and depresses the eye. A right CN IV palsy leaves the right pupil higher than the left, causes difficulty looking down (down stairs, reading), and produces a compensatory head tilt to the contralateral, unaffected side to correct the lost intorsion. These findings localize to the right trochlear nerve.

explanation_incorrect.A: A right CN III palsy would produce ptosis, a dilated pupil, and down-and-out gaze, not an elevated pupil with a head tilt.
explanation_incorrect.B: A right CN VI palsy would leave the right eye unable to abduct and medially displaced, without vertical deviation or head tilt.
explanation_incorrect.D: A left CN IV palsy would make the left eye higher and cause a compensatory head tilt to the right, the opposite of the findings here.
explanation_incorrect.E: A left CN III palsy would affect the left eye with ptosis and a down-and-out gaze, not an elevated right pupil.

educationalObjective: CN IV palsy causes an elevated pupil on the affected side, inability to look down, and a head tilt to the contralateral side.

subject: Neurology
subtopic: Cranial nerve III, IV, VI palsies
vignette: A 60-year-old woman complains that her right eye will not move to the right. On examination the right eye cannot abduct and is displaced medially when she looks straight ahead. All other eye movements and the pupils are normal.
question: Which muscle and nerve are affected in this patient?

options.text: Right medial rectus, CN III
Right superior oblique, CN IV
Right inferior rectus, CN III
Left lateral rectus, CN VI
Right lateral rectus, CN VI

explanation_correct: CN VI innervates the lateral rectus, which abducts the eye. A right CN VI palsy prevents abduction of the right eye, leaving it displaced medially in the primary position of gaze because the unopposed medial rectus pulls it inward. This is consistent with the rule LR6SO4R3.

explanation_incorrect.A: The medial rectus is supplied by CN III and adducts the eye; its weakness would limit inward movement, not abduction.
explanation_incorrect.B: The superior oblique is supplied by CN IV and depresses and intorts the eye; its palsy would elevate the pupil, not impair abduction.
explanation_incorrect.C: The inferior rectus is a CN III muscle that depresses the eye and would not cause a medially displaced eye at rest.
explanation_incorrect.D: A left CN VI lesion would affect abduction of the left eye, not the right eye described here.

educationalObjective: CN VI palsy prevents abduction because the lateral rectus is paralyzed, leaving the eye medially displaced at rest.
